Apply: https://digitalmehmet.com/contact & https://illumination-curated.com Artificial Intelligence Fintech Ai Model Routing Product Strategy Ai Cost Optimisation The AI Org Chart: Why Your Cheapest Model Might Be Your Best Hire Ogbuehi Chijioke 5 min read · Sep 25, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Original AI-generated image created with Microsoft Copilot for “The AI Org Chart: Why Your Cheapest Model Might Be Your Best Hire.” There’s a decision every fintech product team eventually has to make, usually while staring at a usage-and-billing dashboard at 11pm: do we route this task to the frontier model, or the cheap one? It’s tempting to treat this as a technical question. It isn’t. It’s an HR question wearing an API key. Every model is an employee. Some just cost more to keep on staff. Think about how a payments business actually staffs itself. You don’t put your most expensive risk analyst on every transaction that flows through the gateway — most of them are boring, low-stakes, and correctly handled by a junior officer following a checklist. You reserve your sharpest, most expensive minds for the transactions that are ambiguous, high-value, or genuinely strange. The org chart isn’t a hierarchy of who’s “smartest.” It’s a hierarchy of who’s smart enough , deployed against what the task can actually afford. AI models work the same way, and the fintech companies that get this will out-build the ones still treating “call the biggest model for everything” as a strategy rather than a bill waiting to happen. A small, cheap model is your enthusiastic junior officer. Fast, tireless, works for tokens instead of a salary, and perfectly capable of categorising a transaction, drafting a routine merchant email, or flagging that an invoice field is empty. Ask it to reconcile a genuinely ambiguous settlement dispute across three currencies and a stale FX rate, and it will confidently hand you the wrong answer with the same tone it used to get the easy ones right. It doesn’t know what it doesn’t know. A mid-tier model is your competent associate. Good judgement on most things, occasional escalation, reliable enough to run unsupervised on the bulk of your queue. A frontier model is the senior specialist you don’t put on the phones. Expensive per hour, genuinely worth it when the stakes are high or the problem is novel, and a wasteful way to answer “what’s my balance?” The mistake isn’t using cheap models. The mistake is not knowing which employee you’ve hired for which desk. The MSME lesson, applied to compute I’ve spent a lot of time recently thinking about how a merchant-facing AI copilot — one that drafts invoices, watches inventory, flags anomalies in a small business’s transaction stream — should actually be built. The honest answer is: not as one model doing everything, but as a small org chart. Picture a Merchant Copilot sitting inside a payment gateway: Tier 1 — the intern desk. A small, fast, cheap model handles the volume: “generate this invoice,” “confirm this stock level,” “summarise today’s settlements.” Ninety percent of a merchant’s requests live here. This tier should run at a token cost so low you barely notice it in the infrastructure line of the P&L. Tier 2 — the associate desk. A mid-weight model picks up anything with a bit of reasoning attached — spotting that a merchant’s reorder pattern looks off, drafting a dunning message with the right tone for a repeat late-payer, reconciling a multi-line invoice against a partial payment. Tier 3 — the specialist desk. Reserved for the genuinely hard cases: a fraud pattern that doesn’t match any known signature, a merchant dispute with regulatory exposure, a cross-border settlement anomaly that needs real synthesis across policy, currency and history. This is where you spend your expensive tokens, because this is where a wrong answer actually costs you something. The trick — and it’s the same trick every well-run ops team already knows — is the escalation path , not the headcount. A junior officer who knows exactly when to escalate is worth more than a senior specialist forced to personally read every transaction. Build the routing logic (confidence scores, complexity heuristics, a cheap classifier deciding which desk gets the ticket) and you’ve built an AI workforce that scales the way a real back office scales: mostly on cheap, competent labour, with expensive judgement reserved for where it’s earned. This is precisely the kind of routing logic and prompt architecture I walk through, desk by desk, in the AI Producer Starter Kit — a practical build-along for anyone assembling their first tiered AI workflow rather than reaching for one expensive model out of habit. The credit-cost P&L nobody puts in the pitch deck Here’s the part that should make every product and finance leader sit up: token cost is now a genuine line item, not a rounding error. A frontier model can cost ten to thirty times more per request than a lightweight one. Route every merchant query — including “what’s my balance” — through your smartest, most expensive model, and you’ve built a fintech product with the unit economics of a boutique consultancy, not a scalable payments business. Nigerian MSMEs are exquisitely price-sensitive; a merchant tool that’s brilliant but bleeds margin on every free-tier query never survives contact with a real pricing model.
